Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder that is usually due to a defect in the enzyme phenyla- lanine hydroxylase. This results in raised blood concentrations of phenylalanine in the neonate, and if untreated produces a syn- drome of skin rash, depigmentation, hypertonia, seizures, and se- vere mental retardation.5,6 Variants of phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency include atypical or mild phenylketonuria and hyper- phenylalaninaemia; some patients have an inherited defect in the metabolism of tetrahydrobiopterin causing a ‘malignant phe- nylketonuria’.7 The disease is controlled by use of a diet very low in phenyla- lanine,5,8,9 which if started early can permit relatively normal in- tellectual development. Protein substitutes are recommended, but the optimal dose remains to be determined; there is some evi- dence that phenylalanine tolerance increases, and blood phenyla- lanine levels decrease, when total protein intake from the protein substitute is increased.10 Controversy exists as to whether dietary restrictions may eventually be relaxed,7,9 and most consider life- long metabolic control necessary.5,11 Metabolic control is impor- tant in pregnant women as the consequences of fetal exposure to high phenylalanine concentrations include microcephaly, mental deficiency, and congenital heart disease.5,12,13 No consensus exists as to optimal blood concentrations of phe- nylalanine, although frequent monitoring is necessary. In the UK and USA, values between 2 and 6 mg per 100 mL are usually recommended for neonates, children up to age 12, and pregnant women; for patients over 12 years, concentrations between 2 and 10 mg per 100 mL have been advocated.5 High-dose tyrosine does not appear to be an effective alternative to a diet low in phenylalanine.14-18 The active form of tetrahyd- robiopterin, sapropterin (p.2383), has been used, with dietary phenylalanine restriction, neurotransmitter replacement, and fo- linic acid, to treat malignant phenylketonuria;7,19 it has also shown some promise for the treatment of maternal phenylke- tonuria.20 Some have suggested sapropterin may even replace a low-phenylalanine diet in certain patients.21 Enzyme replace- ment or substitution are under investigation
